name: Observer Effect
description: In the social-science sense, people may change their behavior because they know they are being observed or studied. This entry is about behavioral reactivity, not the physics meaning of measurement disturbing a system.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to usability tests, shadowing, field visits, diary studies, analytics instrumentation, and any product research where the act of observation can itself alter the behavior being studied.
myth_risk_note: The original Hawthorne-studies data do not clearly support the popular version of the effect (Jones's reanalysis), but subsequent purpose-designed research (McCambridge et al.'s systematic review, McCarney et al.'s RCT) independently confirms real research-participation effects exist, just via different, heterogeneous mechanisms than the founding anecdote implies.
prevalence_note: One of the most familiar cautions in observational and usability research, though usually discussed under the Hawthorne/reactivity label rather than as a precision behavioral-economics concept.

findings.description: A systematic review of 19 studies concluded that behavior can change because people are taking part in research, answering questions about their behavior, or being directly observed, but the evidence is highly heterogeneous and little can be securely said about the conditions or magnitude of the effect.
findings.source_title: Systematic review of the Hawthorne effect: New concepts are needed to study research participation effects

applications.title: The original Hawthorne Works lighting studies: productivity rose in both directions once workers knew they were being watched
applications.description: 1920s studies at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works factory tested whether workplace lighting affected productivity. A test group's productivity rose when lighting improved -- but it also rose when lighting was made worse, and researchers found the same unexplained productivity increase no matter which variable (pay, break length, etc.) they manipulated. The common factor across every condition was that the test group knew it was being specially observed.
applications.ethical_note: The origin case for observer effects in behavioral research methodology, not a designed influence on a user -- directly relevant to this graph's own user-research practice (why field studies, user testing, and diary studies can all produce inflated results simply because participants know they're being watched), which the source article itself addresses with concrete mitigation methods.

applications.title: TikTok users self-censoring exploration for fear of being watched by the algorithm
applications.description: Users become reluctant to explore content outside their usual feed on TikTok because they know the recommendation algorithm is tracking every video watched and will reshape future recommendations accordingly -- knowing they're being observed changes their behavior, keeping them inside a narrower 'content rabbit hole' than they might otherwise explore.
applications.ethical_note: The platform isn't deceiving anyone about being tracked, but the resulting behavior change (self-censored exploration) is a real cost to users that an opt-in private-browsing mode -- which the source notes a competitor already offers -- could address; worth naming as a real, addressable gap rather than an inevitable tradeoff.
